Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law

immigrant noun

also immigrants, immigration, immigrate, newcomer, incomer, settle in a new country

classical

Verg. E. 9.2 (Lewis & Short)
Cic. de Or. 1.249: peregrīnī atque advenae (Lewis & Short)

advena, advenae m./f.

Declension on Wiktionary

newcomer from elsewhere, incomer, foreigner

One who has come (advenīre) to a place and lives there, as against indigena, a native. Used of birds as well: cranes and storks are advenae (Plin. NH 10.61).

Other words

  • inquilīnus, inquilīnī m. — incomer; someone living in a place not his own

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Sall. Cat. 31.7: inquilīnus cīvis urbis Rōmae (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

    Its everyday sense is a tenant or lodger (see tenant). Sallust’s Catiline sneers at Cicero, born in Arpinum, as a citizen who only lodges in Rome; so of a newcomer to a country it is contemptuous.

  • immigrō, immigrāre, immigrāvī, immigrātum — move in, go to live (in a place)

    verb, first conjugation, intransitive · also used · classical · Cic. Phil. 13.34: in domum et in paternōs hortōs immigrābit (Lewis & Short); Liv. praef. 11 (Lewis & Short) · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    Classically to move into a house or a place, with in and the accusative; to move to a new country it is the same verb, with the country as the place. The simple migrāre is to move house, to emigrate.

Examples

  • Advena est; ē Graeciā hūc migrāvit.

    He’s not from here: he moved here from Greece.composed

See also foreign, tenant, settlement, strange.
